images.caption:
A large cruciform church dating from the twelfth century, although little of this fabric is visible. The oldest part of the church is the base of the tower.
The church consists of nave with north and south aisles and clerestory which extends into the transepts, central tower with north and south transepts (unusually, these are aisled), chancel, west porch, and vestry.
The tower is of three stages, the upper part dates from around 1500 and is topped with eight pinnacles and spirelet. There are 10 bells.
Pevsner dates the bulk of the church to between 1280 and 1330. The nave is older than the chancel, and has six bay arcades. The north transept dates from around 1330, with the south transept a little earlier. The transepts both have three bayed aisles. The clerestory windows were added around 1500, and are all clear glazed. There are 48 in total.
The west porch dates from the early fourteenth century.
There are numerous stained-glass windows and several monuments including the tomb of Lord Mowbray.

The church was restored in the nineteenth century by Gilbert Scott, and has recently also undergone a major restoration including renewing the floor, lighting, organ, and the addition of toilets and kitchen.

images.filename: A country lane right in the heart of our lovely old town - geograph.org.uk - 1317027.jpg
images.caption:
A country lane right in the heart of our lovely old town This was the old Great Northern and London  & North Western joint railway Dated 1879-1964.
At this moment in time, Melton Mowbray Borough Council have offered it up for sale along with adjacent land. A local group (Haven) are fighting to keep it as a nature walk. After all,  that's what it has been since the railway's closure in 1964. If it is sold it will be replaced by a service road to a new retail park, so much for our environmentally friendly council.

images.caption: The Jewry Wall and St Nicholas' Church in Leicester, England. The wall is the second largest piece of surviving civil Roman building in Britain, and is both a Scheduled Monument and a Grade I listed building. Originally it separated the Palaestra from the Frigidarium at Ratae Corieltauvorum's baths. St Nicholas' Church is also Grade I listed, and dates from AD 880.

images.caption: Two old canal-side buildings that are now pubs in the English city of Nottingham. The building to the right is the back of what was the offices of the canal carriers Fellows Morton and Clayton, the front of which now houses a pub that goes by that name. The building with the prominent Fellows Morton and Clayton name painted on it was their warehouse, and now houses a pub called the Canal House. The two narrowboats 'Megan' and 'Tinkers Leen' are part of the Nottingham Narrowboat Project and are seen here moored at their home base.
